title: Campus Bikes II
statement:
A campus is drawn on a 2D grid. `workers[i] = [x, y]` is the position of worker `i` and `bikes[j] = [x, y]` is the position of bike `j`, and there are at least as many bikes as workers.

Give every worker exactly one bike, with no bike shared by two workers (some bikes may stay unused). The distance between a worker at `p` and a bike at `q` is the Manhattan distance `|p[0] - q[0]| + |p[1] - q[1]|`.

Return the smallest possible total of the distances between each worker and the bike they receive.
constraints: All worker and bike positions are distinct
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every way to hand out bikes is a permutation search: up to `10 · 9 · … · 1` assignments. But once some bikes are taken, the best cost of the remaining choices depends only on **which** bikes are taken, not on who took them. If we always serve workers in order `0, 1, 2, …`, a set of taken bikes with `k` members means workers `0..k-1` are done, so the set alone describes the state. With `m <= 10` bikes there are at most `2^10 = 1024` sets, stored as bitmasks.

## Approach

1. `dp[mask]` is the cheapest total for giving the first `used[mask]` workers exactly the bikes in `mask`. Start with `dp[0] = 0`.
2. Visit masks in increasing order; adding a bit always makes a larger number, so every mask is final before it is extended.
3. `used[mask]` (the number of set bits) is the index of the next worker to serve.
4. If all `n` workers are served, `dp[mask]` is a complete assignment: keep the smallest in `best`.
5. Otherwise, for every free `bike`, relax `dp[mask | (1 << bike)]` with `dp[mask]` plus that worker's distance to the bike.

## Example 1, step by step

Workers `(0,0)`, `(2,1)`; bikes `(1,2)`, `(3,3)`. From `mask = 00`, worker 0 takes bike 0 (cost 3) giving `dp[01] = 3`, or bike 1 (cost 6) giving `dp[10] = 6`. From `01`, worker 1 takes bike 1: `3 + 3 = 6`. From `10`, worker 1 takes bike 0: `6 + 2 = 8`. So `dp[11] = 6`, and `best = 6`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(2^m · m): each mask tries each bike once.
- Space: O(2^m) for `dp` and `used`.

## Pitfalls

- Greedily giving each worker the nearest free bike is wrong: an early worker can steal the only good bike of a later one.
- When `n < m`, the answer is not `dp[full]`; it is the minimum over masks with exactly `n` bits.
- Skip masks with `dp[mask] === Infinity`; those bike sets are never reached in order.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n`, `m` | numbers of workers and bikes |
| `full` | number of bike subsets, `2^m` |
| `dp[mask]` | cheapest cost to give workers `0..used[mask]-1` the bikes in `mask` |
| `used[mask]` | how many bikes `mask` holds, which is also the next worker's index |
| `worker`, `bike` | the worker being served and the bike tried for them |
| `next`, `cost` | the mask after taking `bike` and the total it would cost |
| `best` | cheapest complete assignment found |

narration.4: There are 2^m subsets of bikes, each stored as a bitmask.
narration.5: No subset has been reached yet, so every cost starts at Infinity.
narration.7: Giving no bikes to no workers costs nothing.
narration.10: Visit subsets in increasing order, so every subset is final before it is extended.
narration.11: Count the bits: the bit count of mask >> 1 plus the lowest bit.
narration.12: This subset cannot be reached by serving workers in order; skip it.
narration.13: With k bikes taken, workers 0..k-1 are served, so worker k is next.
narration.15: Then this is a complete assignment; keep the cheapest one.
narration.19: Try each bike for the next worker.
narration.20: A bike already in the mask belongs to an earlier worker.
narration.22: The new subset includes this bike.
narration.23: Cost so far plus the Manhattan distance from this worker to this bike.
narration.24: Keep the cheaper way of reaching the new subset.
narration.27: The cheapest complete assignment is the answer.
